newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end mixed as policy debate lingers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end mixed as policy debate lingers.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed mixed Monday after investors spent much of the day on the sidelines amid a lingering debate on what the Federal Reserve will do next with monetary policy, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year T-bond ended up 2/32 at 97-16/32. Its yield remained below the psychological 7.0 percent barier at 6.95 percent.
"There is a debate going on whether the Fed will move ... which kept the market in a very tight range," said Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Corp.
The Fed's policy-setting arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, will meet on September 24 to decide on whether to alter monetary policy or leave it unchanged.

Analysts said the debated flared up after Friday's subdued retail sales and consumer inflation data for August gave many market participants the impression the economy is slowing enough to prompt the Fed to remain on hold.
"I think they're not going to go (with a change in policy)," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

"We now have a deterioration in consumer spending that stretches back three months ... It's not a short-term and can no longer be explained as a fluke or a flash in the pan. It's the real deal," Low added.
August retail sales rose 0.2 percent against expectations of a 0.7 percent rise. Overall consumer inflation rose a tame 0.1 percent, down from forecasts of a 0.2 percent jump.

On the other hand, some analysts still believe the economy might not be weakening enough to bolster the idea that the Fed will keep its federal funds rate target unchanged at 5.25 percent in September.
"I think the Fed is going to go. I wouldn't attach a very high probability to it, but I would lean a little bit more towards them doing something," DLJ's Schaja said.

Analysts mostly agreed, however, the market is fairly priced for now and it should remain in a consolidation mode, mainly because all fresh economic data to be issued later this week are not expected to shed any new light on the current monetary policy debate.
"I think the market is fairly priced right now until we get new evidence ... whether the economy is weaker or stronger," Schaja said.

HSBC's Low added that "basically what it looks like for just about all the indicators between now and the FOMC is that they're mostly second-tier data and just don't have the market moving potential or for that matter the Fed moving potential."
On Monday, the market mostly shrugged off the only economic report scheduled for release during the trading session -- July business inventories.

Inventories rose 0.4 percent in the month, compared to a revised unchanged reading in June. "The inventories had no impact (on the market). We already knew inventories were a bit on the rise in July," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
The three-month Treasury bill closed off two basis points at 5.05 percent. The six-month bill was flat at 5.18 percent. The year bill was down one point at 5.43 percent.

The two-year note closed unchanged at 100-00/32, yielding 6.12 percent. The five-year note traded down 2/32 at 100-1/32 to yield 6.49 percent. The ten-year note closed unchanged at 101-30/32, yielding 6.73 percent.
